title: gpu-memory-fragmentation-and-kernel-restarts-scratch
content:
TL;DR: Intermittent OOMs followed by GPU resets on prod node gpu-b3. Symptoms look like long-running fragmentation of GPU device memory rather than a single allocation exceeding free memory. Host driver/containers seem to have mixed CUDA runtimes (11.8 vs 12.x). Notes of commands tried, outputs captured, and hypotheses below.

Context:
- Node: gpu-b3 (AWS G5.2xlarge equivalent, A10G) running Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.1.0-50-generic.
- Host NVIDIA driver: 535.86.10 (installed via .run in Jan 2025).
- Docker base image: nvidia/cuda:11.8.0-cudnn8-runtime-ubuntu20.04 for many services (mismatch suspect).
- Workload: long-lived batching worker (Redwood-inference runtime) keeps many models loaded, occasionally spawns local eval job (temp heavy allocation).

Observed behavior:
- Gradual increase in fragmented free memory visible in memory maps; small allocations succeed early but larger contiguous allocation fails.
- When failure happens, Xid 79 / GPU hang messages in dmesg followed by kernel marking GPU as reset. Process recovers but model reload slow.
- Sometimes Python raises CUDA OOM despite nvidia-smi reporting a lot of "Free" memory (fragmented).

Commands run and outputs (snippets):
- nvidia-smi (abridged)
  Timestamp: Tue Mar 10 11:02:13 2026
  +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | NVIDIA-SMI 535.86.10    Driver Version: 535.86.10    CUDA Version: 12.1     |
  | GPU  Name        Persistence-M| Bus-Id        Disp.A | Volatile Uncorr. ECC |
  |   0  A10G          On           00000000:00:1E.0 Off |                  N/A |
  |  0%  42C  P8    12W /  150W |   105MiB / 24220MiB |
  +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

- cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version
  NVRM version: NVIDIA UNIX x86_64 Kernel Module  535.86.10  Tue Feb  6 2025
  GCC version:  gcc version 9.4.0 (Ubuntu 9.4.0-1ubuntu1~20.04)

- dmesg | egrep -i "NVRM|Xid|GPU hang|reset" (most relevant lines)
  [ 123456.789012] NVRM: GPU at PCI:0000:00:1e.0 has fallen off the bus.
  [ 123457.001234] NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:00:1e.0): 79, PID=9876, ThreadName=batcher, GPU has fallen off the bus
  [ 123457.001236] nvidia 0000:00:1e.0: GPU has fallen off the bus.
  [ 123457.002000] NVRM: GPU 0000:00:1e.0: GPU firmware fault: reason=MMU fault (0x24)
  [ 123457.100000] Kernel: nvidia: probing for device 0 failed, resetting

- python repro (simple allocation loop to reproduce)
  import torch
  def frag_repro():
      a = []
      for i in range(1000):
          a.append(torch.empty((1024, 1024, 8), device='cuda:0'))  # lots of small blocks
      # then try one large alloc
      b = torch.empty((1, 1024, 1024, 16), device='cuda:0')  # sometimes fails with OOM

  Observed: last line throws RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory.

- torch.cuda.memory_summary() around failure shows high reserved but free blocks in many small chunks (copied locally):
  Allocated: 4.8 GiB, Reserved: 12.1 GiB, Free segments: many small entries (~ <16MB each)

- ldd inside container for libtorch and libcudart (to check which cuda libs linked):
  ldd /opt/conda/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib/libtorch_cuda_cpp.so | grep cuda
    libcudart.so.11.0 => /usr/local/cuda-11.0/lib64/libcudart.so.11.0 (0x00007f...)
  BUT host driver reports CUDA 12.x. So runtime vs driver mismatch present.

- docker run quick checks (container env):
  docker run --rm --gpus all --shm-size=1g nvidia/cuda:11.8-base nvidia-smi
  -> shows driver 535.86.10 and CUDA 12.1 (driver reports supported runtime). Inside container /usr/local/cuda is 11.8 but driver is newer which can support older runtimes.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Memory fragmentation: long-lived allocations + many small allocations create fragmentation on device, making large contiguous allocations fail even when total free >= requested. Certain allocator behaviors (caching allocator in pytorch) exacerbate this.
2) Driver/runtime mismatch causing some libraries to take suboptimal paths or fall back to CPU/old paths that fragment memory or mishandle large pages. ldd shows libcudart from 11.x inside container while host driver is 535 (12.x), which can be fine but could expose edge cases.
3) A GPU firmware or driver bug triggered by specific sequence of API calls => Xid 79/MMU fault. Correlates with model unload/load + pinned memory churn.
4) IPC/shm limits in docker container cause allocations to fail (we saw improvement when increasing --shm-size).

What I've tried (and results):
- Force small changes in allocation pattern (pre-pad with a big contiguous allocation at startup to reduce later fragmentation). Outcome: reduces frequency but does not eliminate.
- Set TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:128 (to limit fragmentation). Outcome: noticeable improvement in preventing large-allocation OOMs in local repro.
- Upgraded pytorch from 1.13 -> 2.1 (many fixes around allocator) on one node. Outcome: reduced occurrence but not eliminated.
- Switched container base image to cuda:12.1-runtime on a canary node to align runtime and driver. Outcome: no GPU resets observed in 72h on canary (promising).
- Increased docker --shm-size to 8g and container run with --ipc=host for the worst-offending service. Outcome: eliminated some OOMs that looked like ipc/shm related.
- Collected minidumps and reported to NVIDIA (case # 2026-03-05-XYZ). NVIDIA response: Xid 79 typically indicates a GPU hang; they asked for system dump + reproducer.

Remaining unknowns / next steps:
- Need to gather systematic traces: periodic check of cuda memory map (via cudaMemGetInfo) and pytorch allocator stats to correlate fragmentation growth over time. Add light-weight sampling to the worker to write stats every minute.
- Roll more machines to container runtime CUDA 12.1 images to remove runtime mismatch variable.
- Try full driver rollback to 520.x on a single node to see whether 535 driver introduced regressions (requires kernel rebuild/maintenance window).
- Build a small reproducer in C/CUDA (not pytorch) that allocates many small buffers and then tries a large one, to see whether allocator implementation (driver vs runtime) is at fault.
- Add watchdog: when a large allocation fails, attempt to trigger a graceful fallback or schedule a model reload on another machine to avoid observed 'GPU reset' cascading impact.

Notes on debugging commands to add to runbook (for SRE oncall):
- dmesg | egrep -i "NVRM|Xid|GPU hang|has fallen off the bus"
- journalctl -k | tail -n 200
- nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY
- python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.memory_summary())" (run inside same conda/env)
- ldd $(python -c 'import torch; import os; print(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(torch.__file__), "lib", "libtorch_cuda_cpp.so"))') | grep libcudart
- lsmod | egrep 'nvidia|nvidia_uvm' ; cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version

Quick mitigation applied so far (summary):
- Canary rollout of cuda:12.1 images (aligned with driver) for batch workers (72h with no resets on 3 canaries).
- Set TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:128 on prod side for offending service (reduced frequency).
- Increased docker shm and used --ipc=host for critical containers.

Other notes / scratch ideas:
- Check which model ops use cuBLAS/cuDNN primitives that allocate large workspace buffers lazily. Maybe pre-warm those workspaces with a one-time warmup that uses contiguous allocation to reduce fragmentation.
- Investigate using CUDA MPS for multi-process GPU sharing (might change allocation patterns).
- Consider runtime-level periodic compaction signals if available (none in CUDA 11/12; but see caching allocator tweaks).

Pinned logs / snippets: (keep for NVIDIA support)
- Full dmesg chunk (attached to JIRA INF-2942)
- Python stack traces for process 9876 (attached)

Bottom line: Likely a combination of allocator fragmentation + runtime/driver interactions. Short-term: continue canary rollout of CUDA 12 images and allocator configs. Mid-term: reproduce in small C repro and coordinate with NVIDIA if we can reliably trigger Xid 79.

Next actions (assigned):
- Maya: add sampling memory_summary to batcher and push canary cuda:12 image to 10% of nodes (due 2026-03-12).
- Diego: prepare minimal C/CUDA reproducer to allocate many small buffers -> one large buffer (due 2026-03-15).
- Sofia: coordinate with NVIDIA case and attach system dump from repair window (in progress).

Scratchpad end.
